title: State Holders, Events, and UI Logic

scout.purpose: This lesson makes state holders, events, and ui logic a concrete production decision rather than a diagram or naming convention.
scout.realWorldUse: Growing Android codebases need this skill to preserve correctness, independent change, testability, and understandable ownership across teams and releases.
scout.outcome: Design and defend the boundary, recognise its failure modes, and verify it with code and evidence.

sections.title: Model the responsibility before the mechanism

blocks.text: State holders have different lifetimes and jobs. A screen-level ViewModel is appropriate for business logic that consumes the data or domain layer and must survive configuration changes. A plain remembered holder can own short-lived UI behaviour such as expanded controls, focus movement, or scroll coordination. A ViewModel should not retain Activity, View, NavController, or other shorter-lived objects. Lifetime alignment is part of correctness, not merely memory hygiene.

blocks.caption: The code exposes the ownership or dependency contract that the architecture must preserve.

sections.title: Make dependency and lifetime rules explicit

blocks.text: Classify each event by origin and consequence. A tap that opens a local help panel is UI logic and can stay in the UI. A tap that submits a payment delegates business policy to the ViewModel or lower layer. If successful submission changes where the user should be, represent the durable business outcome in state and let the UI perform navigation. Channels advertised as guaranteed one-off delivery are fragile when their producer outlives the collector; critical outcomes should not disappear while the app is backgrounded.

blocks.title: Decision lens
rows: A focused test, graph rule, or measurement proves the claim

blocks.text: Not every transient visual needs persistence. A snackbar acknowledging a reversible action may be UI-owned, while a payment rejection must remain visible until the user can act. Define acknowledgement when state contains a consumable message, and include stable identity so recomposition does not repeat it accidentally. Test backgrounding, multiple collectors, configuration recreation, and process restoration. The question is never simply state versus event; it is which outcome must be observable, by whom, and for how long.

Production architecture is evaluated by behaviour under change and failure. Name the owner, lifetime, public contract, cancellation path, and test seam before adding a pattern or framework. Trace one real user action through every boundary, including recreation and alternate implementations. Keep types immutable at consumer boundaries, make dependencies visible in constructors or build files, and prefer a small purposeful abstraction over a generic hierarchy. Record why the choice exists and the evidence that would justify revisiting it. Include privacy, accessibility, observability, and team comprehension in the review because a technically valid graph can still fail its users and maintainers.

steps.detail: Assign one owner and the smallest stable consumer contract.

steps.label: Compose
steps.detail: Connect concrete implementations only at the authorised edge.

steps.label: Stress
steps.detail: Exercise failure, recreation, replacement, and parallel development.

steps.label: Review evidence
steps.detail: Keep, reshape, or remove the boundary based on observed results.

blocks.title: Architecture is not file naming
blocks.text: Watch carefully for this common failure mode in production: Sending successful payment through a non-replayed channel and navigating only if a collector happens to be active.

inspect.title: Inspect the State Holders, Events, and UI Logic boundary
walkthrough: Identify the consumer-facing contract and the concrete implementation or state owner behind it.
Trace dependency direction and confirm that shorter-lived or technology-specific details do not leak outward.
Define a focused test or graph check that would fail if the architectural promise were broken.
inspect.expectedOutput: A small, explainable boundary whose responsibility, lifetime, dependency direction, and verification are explicit.

trap_check.mistake: Sending successful payment through a non-replayed channel and navigating only if a collector happens to be active.
trap_check.why: It obscures ownership or adds coupling without protecting a measurable product or engineering property.
trap_check.fix: Return to the user behaviour, name the invariant and owner, then introduce only the smallest boundary that protects it.

trap_check.mistake: Selecting a pattern or tool before defining lifetime, failure, and replacement behaviour.
trap_check.why: The implementation can compile while recreation, testing, alternate implementations, and team changes remain unsafe.
trap_check.fix: Write the dependency and state contract first, then test it through failure and replacement.

challenge_intro.task: Audit the events in a login and payment flow, assign UI behaviour and business logic to appropriate owners, and prove that critical outcomes survive collector absence.
challenge_intro.successLooksLike: The design has explicit owners and dependency direction, survives its adverse scenarios, and includes evidence for every claimed benefit.

recall.prompt: What problem should state holders, events, and ui logic solve?
recall.answer: They assign business state and short-lived UI behaviour to owners whose lifetimes match the work, without retaining shorter-lived Android objects.

recall.prompt: What makes an architecture boundary trustworthy?
recall.answer: A small explicit contract, controlled dependency direction, and evidence under failure and replacement.

recall.prompt: When should an abstraction or module be removed?
recall.answer: When its navigation and maintenance cost exceeds the protection, reuse, ownership, or measured build value it provides.

objectives: Explain the responsibility and trade-offs in State Holders, Events, and UI Logic.
